sciProEu: Which structure is found in eukaryotic cells but not in prokaryotic cells?
Only eukaryotic cells keep their DNA inside a membrane-bound nucleus; all cells have ribosomes, a membrane and cytoplasm.
Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
Every cell needs ribosomes to make proteins, while mitochondria, nuclei and chloroplasts occur only in eukaryotes.
Which organism is made of prokaryotic cells?
E. coli is a bacterium, and bacteria are prokaryotes; yeast, amoebas and trees are eukaryotes.
Which organism is made of eukaryotic cells?
Mushrooms are fungi, and fungi are built from eukaryotic cells; the others are bacteria.
In a prokaryotic cell, where is the main DNA found?
In a region called the nucleoid
Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so their circular chromosome sits in an unenclosed region called the nucleoid.
Small, circular loops of extra DNA found in many bacteria are called …
Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules separate from the main chromosome, common in bacteria.
Which organelle, found only in eukaryotes, releases energy through cellular respiration?
Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles where eukaryotic cells carry out most of cellular respiration.
What is the shape of the main chromosome in a typical prokaryotic cell?
A double helix inside a nucleus
Most prokaryotes carry one circular chromosome, while eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes in a nucleus.
Which feature do plant cells have that animal cells lack?
Plant cells contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis; animal cells do not, though both have mitochondria, nuclei and ribosomes.
How does the size of a typical bacterium compare with a typical animal cell?
It is exactly the same size
Bacteria are usually 1–5 µm long, while animal cells are usually 10–30 µm across, so bacteria are roughly ten times smaller.
Which structure do bacteria use to swim?
Many bacteria spin a whip-like flagellum to move through liquid.
The cell walls of most bacteria are made mainly of …
Bacterial cell walls are built from peptidoglycan; plant walls are cellulose and fungal walls are chitin.
The cell walls of plant cells are made mainly of …
Plant cell walls are made of the carbohydrate cellulose.
Which statement correctly compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
Both have a cell membrane and cytoplasm
All cells share a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA; the difference is in nuclei and organelles.
Which group of organisms is made entirely of prokaryotic cells?
Archaea, like bacteria, are prokaryotes; protists, fungi and plants are eukaryotes.
A scientist sees a cell with a nucleus, a cell wall and chloroplasts. What kind of cell is it?
A nucleus means eukaryotic, and a cell wall plus chloroplasts point to a plant cell.
A scientist sees a cell with a nucleus and mitochondria but no cell wall. What kind of cell is it?
A nucleus means eukaryotic, and lacking a cell wall points to an animal cell.
A cell has a cell wall, ribosomes and a nucleoid but no nucleus. What kind of cell is it?
A nucleoid with no nucleus means the cell is prokaryotic, such as a bacterium.
Which organelle in eukaryotic cells packages and ships proteins?
The membrane-bound Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins in eukaryotic cells.
Why can eukaryotic cells carry out many processes in separate compartments?
Internal membranes create organelles, so different jobs can happen in separate spaces.
Which structure, made of chitin, surrounds the cells of fungi?
Fungal cells are eukaryotic and are surrounded by cell walls made of chitin.
Which pair is the best example of a prokaryote and a eukaryote?
A bacterium and a human skin cell
A plant cell and a fungus cell
An animal cell and a yeast cell
A bacterium is prokaryotic and a human cell is eukaryotic; the other pairs are all eukaryotes.
sciTransp: Oxygen moves from the lungs into the blood because it is more concentrated in the lungs. This is …
Oxygen spreads from high to low concentration across the membrane without energy, which is simple diffusion.
A red blood cell placed in pure water swells and may burst. Water entered by …
Water moves across the membrane toward the higher solute concentration inside the cell, which is osmosis.
Glucose enters a cell through a carrier protein, moving down its concentration gradient. This is …
Movement down a gradient through a protein, without ATP, is facilitated diffusion.
The sodium–potassium pump moves ions against their gradients using ATP. This is …
Pumping ions from low to high concentration requires energy from ATP, so it is active transport.
A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium by wrapping its membrane around it. This is …
Taking material in by folding the membrane around it is endocytosis (specifically phagocytosis).
A cell releases hormones by fusing vesicles with its membrane. This is …
Vesicles fusing with the membrane to push contents out of the cell is exocytosis.
A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell is called …
Hypertonic means the outside has more solute, so water tends to leave the cell.
A solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell is called …
Hypotonic means the outside has less solute, so water tends to enter the cell.
A cell is placed in an isotonic solution. What happens to its overall water content?
In an isotonic solution water enters and leaves at equal rates, so there is no net change.
A plant cell in fresh water becomes firm. What causes this?
Water enters and pushes on the cell wall
Salt leaves the vacuole by diffusion
ATP pumps sugar out of the cell
The cell wall absorbs all the water
Water enters by osmosis and the swollen vacuole presses on the cell wall, giving turgor pressure.
Lettuce leaves wilt when sprinkled with salt. Why?
Water leaves the cells by osmosis
Salt is pumped in using ATP
Salt makes the outside hypertonic, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis and they lose firmness.
Which type of transport does NOT need a membrane protein?
Uptake of ions by a carrier
Small nonpolar molecules like oxygen slip directly through the lipid bilayer without a protein.
Root hair cells take in minerals from soil where minerals are less concentrated. This must be …
Moving minerals from low to high concentration requires energy, so it is active transport.
Higher temperature makes particles move faster, so they diffuse more quickly.
Which molecule supplies the energy for active transport?
Cells break down ATP to release energy that powers pumps in active transport.
What do diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion have in common?
They are all passive and need no ATP
They all need ATP from the cell
They all move against a gradient
All three move substances down a concentration gradient without the cell spending energy.
Water passes quickly through special channel proteins called …
Aquaporins are channel proteins that let water molecules cross the membrane rapidly.
A drop of food colouring spreads through still water. This is an example of …
The dye particles spread from high to low concentration on their own, which is diffusion.
A cell takes in droplets of fluid by pinching off small pockets of membrane. This is …
Pinocytosis, or 'cell drinking', is endocytosis of fluid in small vesicles.
Carbon dioxide leaves body cells and enters the blood. It moves by …
CO₂ is more concentrated in cells than in blood, so it diffuses out without energy.
Why is the cell membrane described as selectively permeable?
It lets some substances through but not others
It lets every substance through freely
It only allows water to pass
The membrane controls traffic, allowing some molecules across while blocking others.
Which form of transport moves substances from high to low concentration?
Facilitated diffusion moves substances down their gradient; pumps move them against it.
sciXsCarbBio: What gas do plants take in to make glucose during photosynthesis?
Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen

Transpiration

Oxygen
Nitrogen

Rocks
Volcanoes
Glaciers

Respiration and decomposition

Something that absorbs more carbon than it releases
Something that releases more carbon than it absorbs
A machine that makes carbon
A place with no carbon at all
A sink, such as a growing forest, takes in more carbon than it gives off.
Which of these is a carbon sink in the biosphere?
A growing forest
A forest fire
A coal power plant
A herd of cattle
A growing forest absorbs more CO₂ through photosynthesis than it releases.

It turns into oxygen gas

They release no gases at all

Which product of photosynthesis stores carbon?
Glucose
Oxygen
Water
Sunlight

The mitochondrion
The cell wall

By photosynthesizing at night
By absorbing CO₂ through its fur

What role do earthworms play in the carbon cycle?
They break down dead matter and mix it into soil
They photosynthesize underground
They create carbon from nothing

Which organisms are decomposers in the carbon cycle?

Grasses and trees
Hawks and owls
Algae and mosses

How can planting crops that cover soil year-round help the carbon cycle?

sciXsCarbGeo: Coal formed from swamp plants buried and compressed for millions of years.
Oil and natural gas formed mainly from …
Oil and gas formed from plankton buried in ocean sediments and heated under pressure.
Which rock is mostly made of calcium carbonate?
Limestone is a sedimentary rock made largely of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
How does the ocean exchange carbon with the atmosphere?
CO₂ dissolves into and escapes from seawater
The ocean turns CO₂ into nitrogen
CO₂ dissolves at the ocean surface and can also be released back to the air.

Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH.

It makes building carbonate shells harder
It makes their shells grow thicker
It turns their shells into oil
More acidic water reduces the carbonate available, so shells are harder to build and may dissolve.

Heating limestone breaks down CaCO₃ into lime and CO₂, releasing carbon to the air.

Rock formation, weathering and plate movement move carbon very slowly, over millions of years.

Burning coal, oil and natural gas
Burning fossil fuels quickly releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years.
How does carbon in subducted rock return to the atmosphere?
Subducted rock melts deep underground, and volcanoes release some of its carbon as CO₂.
Which fossil fuel is mostly methane?
What are the Alberta oil sands an example of?
A store of carbon in the geosphere
A store of carbon in the air
The oil sands hold bitumen, a fossil fuel that stores ancient carbon underground.
Which process slowly turns buried organic matter into fossil fuels?
Burial adds heat and pressure that slowly change organic matter into coal, oil and gas.
How do rivers carry carbon from rocks to the ocean?
They carry dissolved minerals from weathering
They pump CO₂ into the air
Weathering dissolves carbon-containing minerals, and rivers carry these ions to the sea.
Which material forms when CO₂ dissolves in rainwater?
CO₂ reacts with water to form weak carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which helps weather rock.
What is carbon capture and storage?
Trapping CO₂ and pumping it underground
Burning more coal to make CO₂
Carbon capture and storage collects CO₂ from sources like power plants and stores it in rock layers.
Why does the deep ocean store carbon for a long time?
Deep water mixes with surface water slowly
Deep water has no dissolved gases
Carbon that sinks to the deep ocean can stay there for centuries because deep water circulates slowly.
Which rock forms from layers of shells pressed together on the sea floor?
Shells of calcium carbonate pile up and are cemented into limestone.
Which part of Earth holds carbon as diamonds and graphite?
Diamond and graphite are pure carbon minerals found in rocks of the geosphere.
How does weathering of rock over millions of years affect atmospheric CO₂?
It slowly removes CO₂ from the air
It quickly adds CO₂ to the air
It has no effect on CO₂

Where does most carbon in a volcanic eruption come from?
Rocks and magma deep inside Earth
Volcanic CO₂ comes from melted rock and magma below Earth's surface.
Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?

They form again within a week
Fossil fuels form far more slowly than we use them, so they cannot be replaced on a human time scale.
sciXsSolarObj: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
Iron oxide (rust) in its soil gives Mars its reddish colour.
Venus's thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury.
Which planet is farthest from the Sun?
Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet from the Sun.
Which planet spins on its side, with its axis tilted about 98°?
Uranus is tipped so far that it rolls around the Sun on its side.
What is the largest moon in the solar system?
Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is the largest moon and is bigger than Mercury.
Which moon of Saturn has a thick atmosphere?
Titan is the only moon known to have a thick atmosphere, mostly nitrogen.
What are the four inner planets called?
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars have solid rocky surfaces, so they are terrestrial planets.
Which two planets are called gas giants?
Jupiter and Saturn are huge planets made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
Which two planets are called ice giants?
Uranus and Neptune contain a lot of water, ammonia and methane ices.
A small rocky piece of debris travelling through space, smaller than an asteroid, is a …
A meteoroid is a small space rock; it becomes a meteor when it burns in the atmosphere.
A distant shell of icy bodies around the solar system
A cloud of gas inside Jupiter
A belt of rocks between Earth and Mars
A ring of dust around Saturn
The Oort Cloud is a far-off spherical region of icy objects thought to be the source of long-period comets.
Which dwarf planet lies in the asteroid belt?
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is classified as a dwarf planet.
Which object is the largest in the solar system?
The Sun holds over 99% of the solar system's mass and is far bigger than any planet.
Which planet has the Great Red Spot, a giant storm?
The Great Red Spot is a huge, long-lasting storm on Jupiter.
Which planet is our nearest neighbour and is similar in size to Earth?
Venus is close to Earth's size and comes closer to Earth than any other planet.
Moons are natural satellites because they orbit planets without being made by people.
Solar wind and sunlight push a comet's gas and dust away from the Sun.
What are Saturn's rings made of?
Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock, from dust-sized to house-sized.
Which object in the solar system makes its own light?
The Sun is a star that produces light by fusion; planets and moons only reflect sunlight.
Which planet has the shortest year?
Mercury is closest to the Sun, so it completes an orbit in only about 88 Earth days.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Which object orbits the Sun but has not cleared other objects from its orbit?
A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is round but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
sciXsStars: Which colour of star has the lowest surface temperature?
Red stars are the coolest, at about 3000 °C, while blue stars are the hottest.

The Sun's surface is about 5500 °C, which gives it a yellow-white colour.
The hot, dense core left after a Sun-like star dies
A young star still forming in a nebula
A giant star about to explode

The birth of a small star

They have less fuel to start with

A star that has swollen as it ages
A newborn star in a nebula
The core left after a supernova

How bright a star looks from Earth

How old a star really is
How far a star has travelled

How bright a star would look from a standard distance
How bright a star looks from Earth tonight
How hot a star's core is
How large a star's planets are

A young star forming before fusion begins
A dead star made of neutrons
A star in the middle of its life

On the H-R diagram, where are hot, bright stars found?

Which star is the closest to Earth?

What is a binary star system?
In a binary system, two stars orbit a common centre of mass.

The colour and shape of objects

The amount of matter in an object
The space an object takes up

Earth's gravity constantly pulls the Moon toward it, curving its path into an orbit.

What type of reaction is this? Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag
Copper replaces silver in the compound, which is single replacement.
What type of reaction is this? Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
Chlorine replaces bromine in the compound, which is single replacement.
What type of reaction is this? Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
Magnesium replaces hydrogen in hydrochloric acid: single replacement.
What type of reaction is this? 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
Sodium replaces one hydrogen in water and frees hydrogen gas: single replacement.
What type of reaction is this? BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl

What type of reaction is this? HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O
An acid and a base exchange ions to form a salt and water: double replacement.
What type of reaction is this? Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ + 2KNO₃

What type of reaction is this? A + B → AB
Two substances combining into one product is synthesis.

One substance breaking into two is decomposition.
What type of reaction is this? A + BC → AC + B
One element takes the place of another in a compound: single replacement.
What type of reaction is this? AB + CD → AD + CB

Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so two units is 10 × 10 = 100 times.

What colour does red litmus paper turn in a base?

Acids increase the concentration of hydrogen (hydronium) ions in water.

Which compound is a common acid?

sciXsNewton: A car turns sharply left and a passenger slides toward the right door. Why?
Their body tends to keep moving straight
The door pulls them toward it
Gravity pushes them sideways

Zero
Forward
Backward
Upward

Its colour
Its temperature
Its shape

inertia
acceleration
action and reaction
gravitation

Slow down and stop
Speed up forever
Roll backward

Gravity stops working on the bottle

Zero
Upward
Downward
Sideways

Downward
Upward
Sideways

Space pushes it along

A bowling ball
A brick
A car

Yes, a constant forward force
Yes, a constantly growing force
No, but it slows on its own

Galileo Galilei
Charles Darwin
Marie Curie
Dmitri Mendeleev
